extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying patent litigation evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing admissibility and proof of prior use, abandonment, state-of-the-art evidence, witness competency and credibility, judicial notice, and expert testimony in patent infringement actions in U.S. courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of prior use must extend to the entire claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The allegations of the notice must not be limited to one or more of the elements of which the patented art or article consists, but must extend to the entire invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice that only points to individual elements is insufficient; notice must cover the whole invention as claimed (see cited authorities such as Evans v. Eaton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of knowledge/use in notice need not be specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of such knowledge and use need not be stated except by the general averment that it preceded the inventive act of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general averment that the knowledge/use preceded the patentee's inventive act is adequate; precise dating is not required by the rule quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice must name witnesses to their own prior use/knowledge (names and residences)
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'witnesses, of names and residences of witnesses' is meant the testifier to his own prior use or prior knowledge; the notice should give the names and residences of such witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The witness to be named is the person who can testify to his own prior use/knowledge; the listing should allow the patentee to know who will testify of prior use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice need not name the original inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: That notice of prior use need not name the original inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is sufficient to identify witnesses of prior use rather than attempt to identify any original inventor (see Evans v. Kremer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place-identification in notice must be sufficiently definite
rubrics_metrics.description: That to give the name of a county as the place of knowledge or use is not sufficiently definite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere county may be too vague; naming certain establishments or particular places (e.g., certain mills) in a county may be sufficient in some cases (see Smith v. Frazer; Phillips v. Page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming persons 'of a certain place' without specifying the place is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: That a notice naming persons as of a certain place but not a place is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must adequately describe place of use; merely saying persons are 'of a place' without specifying the actual place can be defective (see Searls v. Boatton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice need not state time of witness's knowledge/use when witness is named with residence and place of use
rubrics_metrics.description: That the notice need not mention the time when the witness knew or used, but only his name and residence and the place of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time details are unnecessary if the notice gives the witness's name, residence, and place where the use/knowledge occurred (see Phillips v. Page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior use/knowledge inadmissible without proper notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither a prior publication, nor a patent, nor a rejected application, can be offered to prove use or knowledge by the author, patentee, or applicant, unless preceded by the proper warning to the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant seeks to prove prior use/knowledge by offering such materials as publications or patents, proper statutory/ procedural notice must have been given or the evidence will be excluded (see Marks v. Fox and other cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: No notice required when plaintiff (or licensee) was the prior user
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the plaintiff or his licensee was himself the prior user, and is now endeavoring to enforce a patent obtained by one whom his own acts have anticipated, no notice of such prior use is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defendant need not give notice to prove prior use attributable to the plaintiff or his licensee; the exception recognizes the plaintiff's own prior acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of abandonment to public varies by nature of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of abandonment also differs according to the nature of the evidence to be adduced. Abandonment by public use or sale and abandonment by general conduct, though not distinct defenses, are widely separated by the conclusive presumption attaching to the acts which constitute the former, and the defendant is required in his notice to specifically point out which of these two methods of abandonment he intends to prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If relying on both modes of abandonment, they must be separately alleged; a simple notice of general conduct need not give particulars, but public use/sale must be specially alleged (see Jones v. Sewall, Bates v. Coe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of public use or sale must allege occurrence more than two years before application
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of abandonment by public use or sale must aver that such sale or use occurred more than two years before the application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A notice of use/sale less than or equal to two years before application may be insufficient; conversely, alleging use more than two years before the applicant's invention (i.e., by the patentee) is improper as a defense (see Agawam Co. v. Jordan and related authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: A notice of public use/sale in proper form precludes evidence of prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Under a notice of public use or sale in proper form, evidence of prior use is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defendant properly pleads public use/sale as the abandonment ground, extraneous proof of prior private use may be excluded as duplicative or improperly pleaded (context and cases cited illustrate boundaries of admissibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of the state of the art admissible without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: No notice is required in order to admit evidence concerning the state of the art at the date when the inventive act of the patentee is claimed to have been performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-of-the-art evidence serves to define the exact scope of the alleged invention by comparing prior art to the invention; such evidence may disclose want of novelty but is not excluded for that reason (see Stevenson v. Magowan, Eachus v. Broomall).

rubrics_metrics.name: State-of-the-art evidence limited to defining scope; cannot be used to prove prior use absent notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Such evidence may actually disclose an entire want of legal novelty in the alleged invention, but this constitutes no reason for excluding it, although the court will not permit the defendant to derive any advantage from it upon that defence. Evidence not having the effect of showing the state of the art, though offered for this purpose, is not admissible unless the proper notice has been served.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants may introduce patents, instruments, or articles to show state of the art without notice, but cannot use those same items to prove prior use/abandonment unless they have given the required notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patents admissible without notice to show state of the art but not to prove prior use or priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents issued before the date of the invention may be proved by the defendant, without notice, in all cases where they tend to throw light upon the art to which the patented invention appertains. A patent not set up in the answer cannot be admitted to show priority, but only the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior patents can be used to construe the present patent and show prior art, but if defendant wants to rely on a patent to assert priority (i.e., as anticipatory prior use), it must be properly pleaded/noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publications generally are not admissible to show state of the art without notice
rubrics_metrics.description: That prior publications cannot be offered to show the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts with prior patents — courts have treated published materials differently; check authorities (e.g., Westlake v. Cartter) for limits on relying on publications without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of evidence in patent infringement actions follow ordinary federal/state rules, with patent-specific exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of evidence in actions for infringement are, in their general character, identical with those by which the Federal courts are guided in other suits at law. The various issues in patent litigation differ so widely that in their details those rules now constitute a peculiar and distinct department of practical jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent cases follow common evidentiary principles but have many specialized precepts developed in decisions — lawyers must apply general and patent-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts apply local state evidence rules unless modified by federal law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary Act of 1789 provided that the rules of evidence prevailing in each State should be applied in actions at common law in the Federal courts held within that State, except when otherwise required by the Constitution, treaties, or statutes of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competency and other witness rules are often determined by state law as incorporated by federal statutes, subject to federal exceptions enacted later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts take judicial notice of six classes of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: All courts of common law jurisdiction take judicial notice of six classes of facts: (1) political facts; (2) legal facts; (3) official facts; (4) public history; (5) natural history; (6) the vernacular language, or the meaning of all common English words, and of such terms of art as are in common use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial notice allows courts to accept these facts without evidence; examples include existence of nations, laws, public offices, common words and technical terms in ordinary use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will judicially notice objects in common use in the arts and ordinary scientific knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: They also take judicial notice of all objects in common use in the arts, and of all matters of ordinary knowledge, including matters of science, but not of the substantial differences between the successive conditions of the same material in the various stages of its manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A court may rely on common mechanical knowledge to aid in defining scope of a patent; it will not, however, judicially notice fine technical differences that require proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts may refresh recollection from recognized authorities and take notice of public notoriety affecting patent rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may refresh their recollection by any safe means, and will take judicial notice of matters of public notoriety affecting the right of the applicant to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges can consult authoritative sources to refresh memory; matters generally known publicly (e.g., widely known facts about an industry) can be noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demurrer dismissal only in perfectly clear cases of non-patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: That a court will not dismiss on demurrer for non-patentability unless the case is perfectly clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are reluctant to decide non-patentability on demurrer; only where the lack of patentability is manifest will dismissal be warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency of witnesses mainly governed by state law; generally any person of sufficient age and mental capacity is competent
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person of sufficient age and mental capacity is a competent witness in an action for infringement, unless the laws of the State in which the court is held exclude him on some other ground than that of interest or color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts follow state competence rules (subject to federal modifications); historic disqualifications (e.g., interest) have been relaxed though interest still affects credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest affects credibility but not necessarily competency
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging of the credibility of a witness, the jury may consider his interest in the cause ... The interest which formerly disqualified altogether still weakens the effect of testimony, and ought to exercise a potent influence on the judgment of a jury when evidence proceeding from individuals once incompetent to testify is contradicted by evidence to which no corresponding imputation is attached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties, employees, or others with stake in outcome are competent but their testimony is for the jury to evaluate for bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility measured by ability and disposition to disclose truth (perception, memory, language)
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of a witness is measured by his ability as well as his disposition to disclose the truth. His ability depends upon the accuracy of his perceptions, the retentiveness of his memory, and his power to embody his recollections in suitable expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly in patent cases, familiarity with the invention, habit of observation, and technical vocabulary strongly influence the weight of testimony; courts warn juries about overreliance on long-ago recollections of complex machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior use often uncertain and should be treated with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: No question presents a greater difficulty than that of prior use, where the art or article by which the patented invention is claimed to have been anticipated has passed out of existence, and remains only in the memories of those who saw or used it. Unless the invention were so simple or so universal ... no great reliance can be placed on any impressions they may have concerning its identity with the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts frequently caution juries against undue dependence upon uncertain memory-based evidence of prior use; corroboration and exhibits increase weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witnesses are generally essential in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In most patent cases expert evidence is, and must always be, indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts are admitted to testify though partisan; their opinions are considered with the reasons given and are for the jury to accept or reject. Ex parte expert affidavits are of little value; experts must be skilled in the relevant science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experts' opinions are to be weighed by jury; experts need technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: No person is an expert unless skilled in the science involved. The patent-expert's opinion is received in evidence only in connection with the reasons on which it is based, and is to be accepted or rejected by the jury according to their own view of its fallacy or truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts serve as guides not judges; courts recognize partisan tendencies of experts and assign their testimony appropriate weight; where opposing experts base opinions on same data they usually agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony description of role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent-expert, considered in his real character, is an explorer, gifted with unusual powers of discernment and apprehension; a chronicler ... an expositor ... a monitor ... His relation to the jury is not unlike that which counsel sustain to the court, as guides to a correct decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe judicial functions to experts; their role is to explain facts and suggest conclusions, but the jury determines ultimate issues of fact and effect.
